overview: Adal was a Muslim sultanate in the Horn of Africa, connected with the Gulf of Aden coast and the Harar plateau. Its principal centres included Dakar and later Harar. Cities and communities continued as political authority changed.

periods.title: A changing regional sultanate
periods.summary: Adal linked coastal and inland territories. Dakar preceded Harar as a principal centre; the name’s regional use was broader than any single city.

periods.title: Harar as a capital
periods.summary: Harar served as a political centre. Its commercial and religious core, connected by narrow lanes, forms the basis of the city’s surviving sixteenth-century layout.

periods.title: Harar after Adal
periods.summary: Harar continued as a centre of commerce and Islamic learning, becoming an independent emirate. This later urban history belongs to institutions beyond the earlier sultanate.

periods.title: A living historic city
periods.summary: Harar Jugol became a World Heritage site in 2006. Its residents maintain a living city and cultural traditions.

items.text: Harar’s narrow lanes connect houses with a central concentration of religious and commercial buildings. Five historic gates corresponded to routes into the city and its neighbourhoods.

Traditional Harari houses and their decorated interiors remain distinctive. Later Indian merchants introduced verandas, and builders combined the two traditions. Surviving houses therefore preserve several periods, not one Adal-era design.

Excavations at Harar recovered cattle, goat and sheep bones, along with other animals. Cattle were the most frequent domestic species among identified fragments. These deposits span several centuries, so the sample cannot define a single meal or an exclusively Adal-era diet.

Many cattle survived to adulthood, while goats at Harar were less often slaughtered young than those at the earlier town of Harlaa. Researchers interpret this as greater emphasis on maintaining herds. Bone ages reveal choices in animal management, rather than recipes.

Harlaa’s excavated trade goods and imported marine fish should not simply be transferred to Harar’s story. Harar’s studied assemblages contained no fish bones and few luxury imports. Neighbouring towns had distinct histories and material economies.

Excavations at six mosques tested traditional foundation dates. The recovered radiocarbon evidence ranges from the late fifteenth to early twentieth centuries. It records different episodes of building and use, not six identical foundation dates.

At Din Agobera, a burial near the prayer niche supplied an early date range, from the late fifteenth to mid-seventeenth century. The excavators infer that the mosque was already present. The burial fill does not directly date its construction.

Later repairs changed Harar’s mosques substantially. At Din Agobera, a lighter corrugated roof replaced the heavy roof formerly supported by pillars. Older-looking buildings may contain materials and layouts from repeated rebuilding.

Aw Meshad’s teaching residence accommodated pupils studying the Quran, law and Arabic. Excavated drainage and floors belong to its later history, with dates in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. They cannot demonstrate an unchanged Adal-era school.
Harari weaving, basket making and bookbinding remain living crafts. Their continuity is part of the city’s heritage; it does not establish an Adal-era date for every surviving technique.

ending.text: In the sixteenth century, military reverses, internal struggles and conflict accompanying Oromo movements weakened the sultanate. Its principal seat shifted toward Aussa, followed by separate Aussa and Harar polities. This political fragmentation did not end Harari urban life or the region’s Muslim communities.
